title: AI Browser Extensions in 2026: Install These, Skip Those
content:
Screenshot of layerxsecurity.com (source)

My view: AI browser extensions deserve more scrutiny than they usually get. I'd be most comfortable with extensions from vendors I already trust and pay, such as Claude in Chrome, and I'd review any "free AI sidebar," "GPT summarizer," or unfamiliar agentic assistant before keeping it: check the publisher, the privacy policy, and the permissions it requests, and remove it if you can't justify them. In LayerX's enterprise data, AI extensions had higher rates of known vulnerabilities and broader permissions than extensions overall, and a free tool with no clear business model can fund itself through your data.

What's Actually Going On

Screenshot of go.layerxsecurity.com (source)

AI extensions are now mainstream - and measurably riskier than everything else in your browser

This isn't a vibes-based warning. LayerX's Enterprise Browser Extension Security Report 2026 found that 99% of enterprise users have at least one extension installed, about 25% have more than 10, and roughly 15% now have an AI extension installed . The risk delta is the part that should stop you: 16.3% of AI extensions had a known CVE versus 10.8% of all extensions (about 50% higher; LayerX's summary states 60%), and AI extensions were nearly 3x more likely to have access to cookies . They're also 2.5x more likely to be able to execute remote scripts, and while 34% of all extensions increased their permissions in the past 12 months, AI extensions were 6 times more likely to have done so .

That last stat deserves more attention. An extension you vetted in January may not request the same permissions in September. And the paper trail is thin: only 28.6% of extensions used in enterprises had privacy policies at all .

The attack surface isn't theoretical - 2026 gave us the receipts

Microsoft warned in 2026 that malicious AI assistant extensions were impersonating legitimate AI tools and harvesting LLM chat histories and browsing data, including full URLs and chat content from platforms like ChatGPT and DeepSeek . Reporting cited approximately 900,000 installs, and Microsoft Defender telemetry confirmed activity across more than 20,000 enterprise tenants (Microsoft Security Blog, March 2026). The Cloud Security Alliance's April 2026 research note makes the uncomfortable point that those installs accumulated because employees pick AI extensions based on store ratings, peer recommendations and marketing claims - and unlike SaaS apps that go through procurement review, extensions install with one click and start touching sensitive data immediately . CSA also flags an earlier case: in July 2025, Urban VPN Proxy quietly shipped code in version 5.5.0 that intercepted AI conversations across eight major platforms.

Why is this so easy? Because of what extensions structurally are. Palo Alto's Unit 42 lays it out plainly: extensions run inside the browser's trusted process and can read and modify web content, intercept network requests, access cookies and talk to external servers . Worse, a hostile extension can route traffic through attacker infrastructure or attach the Chrome Debugger Protocol to read decrypted HTTPS response bodies . HTTPS doesn't save you from something living inside the browser.

Meanwhile, the platforms are absorbing the useful features anyway

Separate from security, a second reason for skepticism is redundancy: browsers are adding the same features themselves. Google wired Gemini 3 directly into Chrome on January 28, 2026, with a persistent sidebar and an agentic feature called Auto Browse , though Auto Browse launched in preview for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the U.S. (Google) . And the standalone-browser bet already claimed a casualty: OpenAI announced in July 2026 that Atlas was being deprecated, scheduled it to stop working on August 9, 2026, and moved browser-based agentic capabilities into ChatGPT and Codex instead .

The counterexample - and it matters - is Anthropic's extension. Claude in Chrome is an extension for paid Claude plans, and its Chrome Web Store listing displayed about 17 million users in early October 2026 (listing).

It's an add-on for paying users. In my view, an extension tied to a subscription, from a vendor with a reputation to lose, is a reasonable model, though not a guarantee of safety.

My Take

Screenshot of unit42.paloaltonetworks.com (source)

I think some "best AI extensions" roundups get this backwards. They rank by feature list - summarize a page, rewrite an email, compare prices - as if those features were scarce. They aren't. Page summarization is increasingly built into browsers themselves; Chrome's Gemini, for example, can summarize pages and videos. In my view, accepting broad permissions such as cookie access for a feature your browser already offers is a poor trade.

Here's my rule of thumb (an opinion, not a guarantee): prefer AI extensions from vendors you already pay and trust, and review permissions before installing any. Claude for Chrome makes sense if you pay Anthropic. Grammarly may make sense if you write for a living; it offers a free plan and paid plans (see its plans page), and its extension needs the same permission review . A paid subscription gives a vendor revenue other than your data, though it is not a security control. A free extension from an unfamiliar developer still has to fund itself somehow, so check its privacy policy.

To the skeptic who says I'm fearmongering: notice that LayerX's data actually undercuts the lazy version of this argument. AI extensions were more likely to be actively maintained than non-AI ones - only 22% unmaintained, versus 40% of extensions overall. The problem isn't abandonware. It's live, actively-updated software with escalating permissions and a direct data pipe to third-party LLM providers. That's a harder problem than "delete the old stuff."

A second point: "AI extension" is not one category. A grammar checker that reads your text box and an agentic assistant that clicks buttons in your logged-in banking tab are not remotely the same risk. LayerX's own recommendation is that AI extensions shouldn't be treated the same as a simple spell-checker, given elevated permissions, faster rate of change, and direct access to sensitive in-browser data. Agree completely - and I'd go further. I'd avoid letting an agent act without your confirmation in a session where money, identity, or account recovery is reachable, because the time saved is small compared with the potential downside.

The Strongest Counterargument

Screenshot of labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org (source)

The best case against me: gatekeeping by subscription is a proxy, not a security control. Big vendors ship CVEs too, paid products get breached, and "only install from companies you pay" conveniently entrenches the incumbents while smothering genuinely better small tools. There are useful niche extensions, such as research clippers or transcript exporters, built by small teams that may never offer a paid plan. My rule filters those out along with the junk. That's a real cost, and I won't pretend otherwise.

I still land where I land, because the asymmetry is brutal. The CSA research note argues that installs like those of the 900,000-install impersonation campaign accumulate because people rely on store ratings and peer recommendations to judge extensions - the exact signals a good indie tool and a malicious clone both display. Until there's a trust signal a normal person can verify quickly, "do I pay this company" is a crude filter: better than none, but not a guarantee.

Bottom Line

If you install extensions casually, do this today: open your extensions page and review each AI extension: remove any you don't recognize or no longer use, and check the publisher and permissions of the rest. Before adding anything new, read the permission prompt; if it wants to read and change data on all sites, plus cookies, for a feature your browser already has, think twice. Microsoft's guidance is likewise to review installed extensions and remove unknown ones. If you manage a team, treat extensions as software that can access production data rather than as a personal preference, and inventory them .

The people who should care most are anyone whose browser holds client data, financial dashboards, or customer records.

FAQ

Are AI browser extensions safe to use at all? It depends on the publisher and the permissions requested. The category-level statistics are a reason for caution: 16.3% of AI extensions carry a known CVE versus 10.8% of extensions overall . Sticking to extensions from vendors you know and pay can reduce risk but does not remove it, so still review permissions.

Do I still need an AI extension if my browser has AI built in? In my view, often not. Chrome now has a Gemini sidebar and Auto Browse built in . Auto Browse was launched in preview for U.S. Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. In my view, summarize-and-rewrite extensions overlap with built-in browser features.

Is ChatGPT Atlas still an option? No. Atlas was scheduled to stop working on August 9, 2026, with OpenAI moving browser-based agentic capabilities into ChatGPT and Codex. Treat any comparison article still ranking it as out of date.

What's the single biggest red flag when installing one? Permission creep. 34% of all extensions increased their permissions in the past 12 months, and AI extensions were 6 times more likely to have done so - so audit quarterly, not just at install.

Correction note (October 2026): This post was revised to soften blanket uninstall advice into a review-and-verify approach, correct the CVE comparison wording (16.3% vs 10.8% is about 50% higher; LayerX states 60%), attribute the 900,000-install figure correctly, and remove figures I could not verify (device count, 37% of organizations, Comet availability, Claude install history, Grammarly plan pricing). Sources: LayerX, Microsoft, Cloud Security Alliance, Google, OpenAI.
